**1. What idea is this showing?**
It shows whether an income check keeps up with US consumer prices, and how that depends on the month you start. The example is "Edna", who starts in January 1949 with a check that rises 2% a year. The checks are drawn as a row of 10 crates. A second person, "Carl", starts in January 1966. Everything is labeled "illustrative" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

**2. What changes over time?**
Edna's story runs 20 years. At year 20, all 10 of her crates are still lit, which I read as her check still keeping up with prices. The last frames put Edna and Carl on one timeline. Her 20-year window runs to 1969 and his runs from 1966 to 1986, so the two overlap in 1966–1969. The caption says "same years of prices: her last, his first." In the final frame Edna's crates are still all lit. I can't tell from the image what happens to Carl's crates.

**3. What does it mean?**
Edna's 2%-a-year check kept pace with inflation for 20 years from 1949, and the caption "kept up: the last start month that did" suggests that was the last start month where it did. Carl and Edna lived through some of the same years of price changes, but those years fall at opposite ends of their 20-year spans. So the same price history can leave two retirees in different places, depending on when they start. The animation is about start date and inflation risk.

**4. What advice, if any, would a viewer take from this?**
The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that a payout with a fixed 2% annual increase isn't guaranteed to keep up with inflation. Whether it does depends on the start date, which no one can pick in advance. For my own quote, that would make me ask how each payout option handles rising prices. That is a question the animation prompts, not a recommendation it makes.

**5. Did the animation itself suggest this, or is it your own conclusion?**
It is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the Edna and Carl comparison and says "history, not a forecast." It never mentions annuity options or tells the viewer what to choose.
